title: Jason Cohen: When to make decisions fast vs. slow
summary: Jason argues decisions should default to fast, because speed accelerates action and learning. He lists the conditions that justify slowing down: irreversibility, huge effort, unfamiliar decision types, unmeasurable progress and imperfect information. He frames these as honest questions, not a scorecard.

principles.text: Default to fast decisions; speed drives action and the feedback loop that out-learns competitors.
principles.quote: Fast decisions leads to rapid action, which accelerates the loop of production and feedback, which is how you outpace and out-learn a competitor, even one that already has a lead.

principles.text: Don't decide now what you'll decide much better later, once you have real customer experience.
principles.quote: If we haven't launched a product yet, we're in no position to decide what the next few features should be; we should launch and earn experience through customer interactions.

principles.text: If a decision costs less to implement than to debate, just do it.
principles.quote: If the effort to implement the decision is smaller than the effort to make a decision, just knock it out.

principles.text: Slow down for irreversible decisions; invest in analyzing upsides and risks.
principles.quote: If you can't easily undo the decision, it's worth investing more effort into analyzing the likelihood of the upsides and risks.

principles.text: Under time pressure, dragging out a decision adds risk by eating implementation time.
principles.quote: time-pressure means the more time you spend deciding, the less time you have for implementation and unanticipated problems, so you're actually adding risk by dragging out the decision.

principles.text: Be more deliberate on decision types your organization has never made before, like pricing or acquisitions.
principles.quote: When the organization has never made this type of decision before, the decision is at great risk, and being more deliberate with research, data, debate, or even outside advice, is wise.
